content.text: An engineer has been asked to investigate and report on the failure of a component. Which row of the table correctly identifies what the engineer would need to do before finalising the report?
Investigate the component's material: No; Redesign the component: Yes; Conduct a simulation of the operational use of the component: Yes; Prepare an initial draft of the report: Yes
Investigate the component's material: Yes; Redesign the component: No; Conduct a simulation of the operational use of the component: Yes; Prepare an initial draft of the report: Yes
Investigate the component's material: Yes; Redesign the component: Yes; Conduct a simulation of the operational use of the component: No; Prepare an initial draft of the report: Yes
Investigate the component's material: Yes; Redesign the component: Yes; Conduct a simulation of the operational use of the component: Yes; Prepare an initial draft of the report: No
Separate what belongs to the investigation stage from what belongs to the design-change stage. Redesigning the component is a response to the findings, not an input needed to establish them.

Then ask which tasks generate evidence or allow the findings to be checked - identifying what the component is actually made of, and reproducing the loading it saw in service both do this, and a draft has to be written and reviewed before a report can be finalised.
B
Row B is correct: investigate the material (Yes), redesign the component (No), simulate the operational use (Yes), prepare an initial draft (Yes).

items: Investigate the component's material - YES. A failure investigation has to establish what the component was made from and whether the specified material was actually used, because material defect or substitution is a common root cause.

Redesign the component - NO. Redesign is a corrective action that may follow the investigation and is often reported as a recommendation. It is not a prerequisite for writing the report on the failure.

Conduct a simulation of the operational use - YES. Modelling the loads, temperatures and duty the component actually saw tests the failure hypothesis and shows whether the service conditions explain the failure.
Prepare an initial draft of the report - YES. A draft is needed so the findings can be reviewed, checked and restructured before the report is finalised.
Row A is wrong because it says the material need not be investigated.
Row C is wrong because it says no simulation of the operational use is needed.
Row D is wrong because it says the report need not be drafted before it is finalised.
1 mark: selects the row that requires the material to be investigated, a simulation of operational use and an initial draft — but not a redesign — before the report is finalised

questions.notes: Body defect: the stored body contains only the statement that a scaffold with diagonal braces is shown - the question stem itself is missing, and the options are the bare pairs of load types. The figure confirms the brace is one of a pair of crossing diagonals in a scaffold bay, so the intended question is which two stresses the brace carries. Solved from the figure; the answer is unaffected.

content.text: The diagram shows a scaffold with diagonal braces.

content.alt_text: Scaffold frame with horizontal members and diagonal cross-bracing, with the brace identified by a leader label.

content.text: The diagonal braces of the scaffold are subjected to
Torsion and shear
Torsion and tension
Compression and shear
Compression and tension
A pin-jointed diagonal is a two-force member: the only load it can carry is an axial force along its own length, so shear and torsion are impossible in it.
Imagine the frame trying to rack (lean) to one side. What happens to the two opposing diagonals on either side of that lean - does one get squashed and the other stretched?
D
The braces are subjected to compression and tension (option D).

The scaffold frame is braced so that it cannot rack into a parallelogram. The horizontal ledgers and the vertical standards alone have no resistance to this movement, so the load path for sway is through the diagonal braces. A diagonal is a slender pin-jointed member, so it can only carry an axial force.

When the frame leans to the right the diagonal on the right-hand side of each braced bay is shortened and goes into compression, while the opposing diagonal is stretched and goes into tension. The two form a couple that opposes the sway. Reversing the direction of lean swaps the two, which is why the braces are described as carrying both compression and tension.

items: A (torsion and shear) and C (compression and shear) - a slender brace pinned at both ends cannot be twisted or sheared; it is loaded along its axis only.
B (torsion and tension) - torsion is impossible in a two-force member, and it omits the compression case entirely.
1 mark: identifies that the diagonal braces are subjected to compression and tension

assets.alt_text: Scaffold frame with horizontal members and diagonal cross-bracing, with the brace identified by a leader label.

questions.notes: Body defect: the stored body contains only the statement that a pulley system is shown - the question stem (asking for the mechanical advantage) is missing and the options are bare numbers. Verified against the source figure, which is a two-sheave tackle with four rope segments bearing on the moving block, so the answer is unaffected.

content.text: A pulley system is shown.

content.alt_text: Block and tackle with a fixed upper sheave block and a moving lower sheave block; the effort E is applied to the free end of the rope and the load L hangs from the moving block.

content.text: What is the mechanical advantage of this ideal pulley system?

The mechanical advantage of a pulley system is the number of rope segments that directly support the moving block. Trace the rope from the effort all the way round and count the segments that leave the moving block.

Each supporting segment carries the same rope tension, so the load is shared between them and the effort is the load divided by that count. A fixed sheave only changes the direction of the pull and adds nothing to the advantage.
C

Trace the rope: it leaves the effort, passes up and over the sheave in the fixed upper block, runs down and around the sheave in the moving lower block, and returns up to the block. Four separate rope segments bear on the moving block.
The mechanical advantage is 4, which is option C.

items: A (2) - that is a single fixed sheave used only to change the direction of the effort. With one moving sheave present the count is at least 3.

B (3) - this is what you get if the dead end of the rope is anchored to the fixed block, leaving only three segments on the moving block. In this system the fourth segment also bears on the moving block.
D (5) - two sheaves cannot produce five supporting segments; an odd count is only possible if the dead end is anchored to the moving block of a larger system, which is not the case here.
1 mark: counts the rope segments supporting the moving block and gives the mechanical advantage as $4$

assets.alt_text: Block and tackle with a fixed upper sheave block and a moving lower sheave block; the effort E is applied to the free end of the rope and the load L hangs from the moving block.

content.text: A line specified in AS 1100 is shown.

content.alt_text: A horizontal chain line alternating long and short dashes with heavier strokes at each end.

content.text: Which type of line is shown?
Centre-line
Cutting plane
Hidden feature
Fictitious outline
Line type in AS 1100 encodes meaning, not shape. A dashed line means a hidden feature; a thin chain line means a centre-line or a fictitious outline; a chain line marks a change of section.
The decisive test here is the line WEIGHT. Compare the thickness of the line at its two ends with the thickness in the middle of the run - that is what separates a cutting plane from a centre-line.
B
The line is a cutting plane line (option B).

A cutting plane (or cutting plane) line is a THICK chain line: a long dash, a short dash, a long dash, and so on, with the strokes at each END thickened to mark the limits of the cut. It is usually finished with arrowheads and letters identifying the view taken.

items: A (centre-line) - a centre-line is a chain line of UNIFORM thin weight with no heavy end strokes, and the sequence of its dashes is a long-short-long-short pattern.
C (hidden feature) - a hidden detail is shown with a thin dashed line of short, evenly spaced dashes. This line is a chain line (alternating long and short dashes), not a dashed line.
D (fictitious outline) - the conventional intersection between two surfaces is a thin chain line, again of uniform weight with no heavy ends.

content.text: The heavier strokes at each end of the chain line are the give-away: only the cutting plane line is drawn that way.

items: 1 mark: identifies the line as a cutting plane line

assets.alt_text: A horizontal chain line alternating long and short dashes with heavier strokes at each end.

content.text: Two types of bridge are shown.

content.alt_text: Bridge 1: a deck carried on a thin arch rib with slender spandrel columns. Bridge 2: a masonry arch bridge built of voussoir blocks between stone abutments.

content.text: Which option correctly identifies Bridge 1 and Bridge 2?
Suspension bridge and masonry arch
Suspension bridge and masonry beam
Reinforced concrete arch and masonry arch
Reinforced concrete arch and masonry beam

Look at what carries the deck and how the arch itself is built. Cast-in-place concrete with steel reinforcement can be made thin and slender, whereas a masonry arch has to be thick because it carries its load in compression through solid blocks.

The slender columns standing between the deck and the arch rib are called spandrel columns. They are the signature of a reinforced concrete arch - the deck is supported on the columns and the arch, not hung from cables.
C
Bridge 1 is a reinforced concrete arch bridge; Bridge 2 is a masonry arch bridge. That is option C.

items: Bridge 1 - the arch rib is a thin, slender curved member and the deck is carried on a row of spandrel columns standing on the arch, with the spandrel walls filled in between. A thin arch rib standing on its own is only possible in reinforced concrete, because plain masonry would crack; this is the spandrel-braced (T-beam) reinforced concrete arch form.

Bridge 2 - the arch is built up from individual wedge-shaped masonry units (voussoirs) laid in ring courses between heavy stone abutments, with the spandrel filled in solid masonry. Because the load is carried in compression through the voussoir ring, the arch must be thick - exactly what the drawing shows.
Options A and B are wrong because Bridge 1 is not a suspension bridge - there are no main cables or hangers; the deck is carried from below by the arch and its spandrel columns.
Options B and D are wrong because Bridge 2 is clearly an arch, not a beam: the voussoir ring is visible and the deck spans over an opening that the arch closes.
1 mark: identifies Bridge 1 as a reinforced concrete arch bridge and Bridge 2 as a masonry arch bridge

assets.alt_text: Bridge 1: a deck carried on a thin arch rib with slender spandrel columns. Bridge 2: a masonry arch bridge built of voussoir blocks between stone abutments.

content.text: Which device is used to measure the airspeed of an aircraft in flight?
Altimeter
Pitot tube
Wind gauge
Potentiometer

Airspeed is a measure of the airflow relative to the aircraft, so the instrument must compare the pressure of the air brought to rest at a forward-facing opening with the undisturbed static pressure around the aircraft.

The distractors each measure a different quantity: height above the ground, wind speed and direction, and a passive variable resistance. Only one of them works by sensing a pressure difference caused by the aircraft's motion through the air.
B
The pitot tube (option B).

A pitot-static system has a forward-facing probe whose open mouth is held into the oncoming stream. The air is brought to rest at the probe, so the pressure there is the stagnation (total) pressure, which is higher than the surrounding static pressure by the dynamic pressure. The difference is measured and converted to indicated airspeed.

items: A (altimeter) - an altimeter senses the AMBIENT static pressure and converts it to height above sea level. It gives no information about speed.

C (wind gauge) - a wind vane and anemometer measure the speed and direction of the WIND relative to the ground. They do not measure the speed of the aircraft through the air, which is what airspeed means.
D (potentiometer) - a potentiometer is a passive rotary or linear variable resistor used for position sensing and volume control. It is a measuring element in a circuit, not an airspeed sensor.
1 mark: identifies the pitot tube as the device that measures airspeed relative to the airflow

content.text: An arrangement of resistors is shown.

content.alt_text: Two resistors of $100\,\Omega$ in parallel, connected in series with a third $100\,\Omega$ resistor.

content.text: What is the total resistance of this arrangement of resistors?
$33\,\Omega$
$50\,\Omega$

Identify the junctions first. Two resistors whose ends share the SAME pair of nodes are in parallel and combine using the reciprocal rule; anything in line with the combination is in series and is simply added.
Reduce the parallel pair first, then add what is left in series. Be careful not to multiply the series resistor by two by mistake - look at how many separate paths the current can take.
C
Two of the $100\,\Omega$ resistors share both of their nodes, so they are in parallel and must be combined first.
The third $100\,\Omega$ resistor is in line with that combination, so the two are in series and their resistances add.
The total resistance is $150\,\Omega$, which is option C.

items: A ($33\,\Omega$) - this is what you get if all three $100\,\Omega$ resistors are treated as being in parallel, $\frac{100}{3} \approx 33\,\Omega$.
B ($50\,\Omega$) - this stops after reducing the parallel pair and forgets the series resistor.
D ($300\,\Omega$) - this treats all three as being in series.

1 mark: recognises the two parallel $100\,\Omega$ resistors combine to give $50\,\Omega$; adds the series $100\,\Omega$ resistor to obtain a total resistance of $150\,\Omega$; correct final option selected

assets.alt_text: Two resistors of $100\,\Omega$ in parallel, connected in series with a third $100\,\Omega$ resistor.

content.text: In which of the following do all of the processes require plastic deformation to achieve a final shape?
Brazing, casting, rolling
Brazing, soldering, welding
Extruding, casting, forging
Extruding, pressing, rolling
Classify each process before testing it. A shaping process forces the metal to flow plastically; a moulding process fills a cavity with liquid material; a joining process connects two parts.
Only the shaping processes qualify. A useful check: in a bulk forming process the cross-section of the workpiece is the same before and after - nothing is added and nothing is joined.
D

Option D - extruding, pressing and rolling. All three are bulk metal forming (shaping) processes: the workpiece is forced to flow plastically and its cross-section is redistributed to give the required shape.

items: Extrusion - a billet is pushed through a die, so the material must flow plastically.
Pressing - the workpiece is squeezed between dies (forging, deep drawing, closed-die pressing), which requires plastic flow.
Rolling - the workpiece is flattened between rotating rolls, again by plastic deformation.
A - brazing is a permanent joining process (a filler metal is melted into the joint), and casting is a moulding process in which molten metal fills a cavity. Neither needs plastic deformation.
B - brazing, soldering and welding are all permanent joining processes. None of them shapes the metal.
C - casting is a moulding process. The metal is poured or injected into a mould and solidifies in the shape of the cavity; the bulk of the material never deforms plastically.

1 mark: recognises that brazing, soldering and welding are permanent joining processes rather than shaping processes; identifies casting as a moulding process that does not require plastic deformation; selects extruding, pressing and rolling, all of which shape metal by plastic deformation

questions.notes: Body defect: the stored body contains only the statement describing the drop hammer figure - the question stem (asking for the relationship between the drop height h and the impact velocity v) is missing and the options are bare equations. The figure is a drop hammer held a height h above a pile, so the intended question is unambiguous and the answer is unaffected.

content.text: The diagram shows a drop hammer being used to drive a pile into the ground.

content.alt_text: Crawler-mounted drop hammer held a height $h$ above a pile being driven into the ground.

content.text: The hammer falls from rest through a height $h$ and strikes the pile at speed $v$. Which expression gives $h$?

The hammer is released from rest at height $h$ and reaches the pile at speed $v$ under constant acceleration, so this is a kinematic problem. Decide whether to use $v^{2} = u^{2} + 2as$ with $u = 0$ and $a = g$, or the energy relation $mgh = \tfrac{1}{2}mv^{2}$ - they are not the same expression and only one of the printed options has the right form.
As a check, the result must have the dimensions of a length. $g$ is an acceleration and $v$ a speed, so watch which quantity ends up in the numerator.
A
The hammer starts from rest, so $u = 0$, and it falls vertically under gravity with $a = g$, so the linear motion equation applies.
The height is the impact speed squared divided by twice the acceleration due to gravity, which is option A.

items: B ($h = \frac{2g}{v^{2}}$) and D ($h = \frac{2g}{v}$) both put $g$ in the numerator and $v$ in the denominator, which is the ratio inverted. Dimensionally $g/v^{2}$ and $g/v$ are not lengths.
C ($h = \frac{v}{2g}$) is also dimensionally wrong, and it omits the square on the velocity. The velocity must be squared because $v^{2} = 2as$.
1 mark: applies the kinematic relation $v^{2} = u^{2} + 2as$ with $u = 0$ and $a = g$; rearranges correctly to $h = \dfrac{v^{2}}{2g}$ and selects option A

assets.alt_text: Crawler-mounted drop hammer held a height $h$ above a pile being driven into the ground.

content.text: In a ductile material, which two stresses are used to calculate the factor of safety (FOS)?
Working and yield
Working and compressive
Bending and yield
Bending and compressive

The factor of safety compares the worst stress the material can just tolerate with the stress it actually sees in service, so one of the two must be a material property and the other a service condition.

The material property that matters is the one at which the material begins to yield plastically. For a ductile material that is the yield stress, because beyond it the material deforms permanently rather than returning to its original shape.
A
For a ductile material the factor of safety is the ratio of the yield stress to the working (service) stress, so the two stresses are working and yield - option A.

A ductile material warns the designer before it fails: once the yield stress is exceeded it deforms permanently, and the deformation gives visible warning, so yield is chosen as the limiting stress and the yield stress appears in the numerator. (For a brittle material, which gives no warning, the ultimate strength is used instead.)

items: B (working and compressive) and D (bending and compressive) - bending stress and compressive stress describe HOW a load is applied to a member. They are service conditions, not a limit the material can sustain, so they cannot form the numerator of the factor of safety.
C (bending and yield) - mixing a service condition with a material property in the wrong order; the numerator must be the material's limiting stress.
1 mark: identifies $\mathrm{FOS} = \dfrac{\sigma_{\text{yield}}}{\sigma_{\text{working}}}$ for a ductile material

content.text: What is the most appropriate propulsion system for a long-haul commuter aircraft?
Ramjet
Scramjet
Turbofan
Turboprop

First separate the engines that need the aircraft to be moving fast before they will work at all from those that can produce thrust from rest. Then consider the cruise requirement of a long-haul flight: subsonic speed, high altitude, several hours aloft, with limits on fuel burn and noise.
Also consider what happens to a propeller as the aircraft climbs to jet altitudes and speeds - its efficiency falls away, and so does the thrust available.
C
A turbofan (option C) is the most appropriate engine for a long-haul commuter aircraft.

A turbofan contains a compressor, a combustor and a turbine that drive each other, so it is self-sustaining: it produces full thrust on the ground at zero airspeed and all the way through take-off and climb, and then delivers efficient subsonic cruise (typically around $M$ 0.8) at high altitude for several hours. Its specific fuel consumption in cruise is low and the jet noise signature is much lower than a turbojet, both of which matter on a long route.
The by-pass air can also be used to cool the exhaust before mixing, which is a further noise and thrust reduction.

items: A (ramjet) and B (scramjet) - neither has a compressor or turbine; the only energy source is the kinetic energy of the aircraft itself, so they produce no thrust at all on the ground and are useless at the low speeds of take-off and climb. A ramjet works only above about $500\,\mathrm{km/h}$ and a scramjet only at supersonic speeds.

D (turboprop) - efficient and very suitable below about $10\,\mathrm{km}$ altitude and at lower speeds, but a propeller loses efficiency rapidly as the aircraft climbs and accelerates, and propellers are unsuited to the high cruise altitudes and speeds of a long-haul jet service.
1 mark: identifies the turbofan as the most appropriate engine for long-haul subsonic cruise

content.text: Which option shows the development of the transition piece (scale $2:1$)?

content.alt_text: Development A: the four developed faces read X, Y, Z, W from left to right.
Development B: the four developed faces read Y, Z, W, X from left to right.
Development C: the four developed faces read W, X, Y, Z from left to right.

content.text: A development is made by imagining the faces hinged about their shared fold edges and rotated down into the plane of the paper. Work from one fixed face outwards, and keep the true face WIDTHS unchanged - unfolding never stretches or shrinks a face.

The fold angle between two developed faces is not free either: it is set by the angle between those two faces on the solid. Compare the angle at each fold in your unfolding with the angle at the corresponding edge of the transition piece.
A
Unfolding about the fold edges in the order X, Y, Z, W (working from the top face outwards, with each new face reflected across its shared fold line) gives development A.

Two checks confirm it. First, the four face widths in development A match the true widths of faces X, Y, Z and W on the isometric - a development must not resize a face. Second, the angle at which each face meets the previous one across its fold line reproduces the dihedral angle of the corresponding edge on the solid.

B, C and D show the same four faces in the same cyclic sequence, so the face order alone cannot distinguish them. They differ in the ANGLES at which the faces are laid out: the faces are rotated to the wrong angle about their fold lines, so they neither lie flat as the solid dictates nor keep the true face relationships. Only A is consistent with the transition piece.

content.text: Which statement best describes modulation?
The addition of information to a carrier wave.
The attenuation of information in a carrier wave.
The removal of quantised information from a carrier wave.
The filtering of unnecessary information from a carrier wave.

Modulation exists so that a low-frequency information signal can be sent on a high-frequency carrier that is efficient to transmit. Ask what is being CHANGED in the carrier, and in which direction the change is made.

Two of the options describe losing or removing something from the signal, and one describes cleaning up an unwanted component at the receiver. Only one option describes a process that builds the information INTO the carrier.
A
Modulation is the addition of information to a carrier wave - option A.

The information signal (voice, data, video) is combined with a high-frequency carrier so that the transmitted signal is band-limited to a frequency band in which the transmission path is efficient and the receiving aerial can be made small. In analogue modulation the amplitude, frequency or phase of the carrier is varied in step with the information; in digital modulation a carrier is switched on and off in coded groups (ASK, FSK, PSK). Either way the process ADDS information to the carrier.

items: B (attenuation) - attenuation is the LOSS of signal strength with distance through the medium. It reduces the information and is the opposite of what modulation does.
C (removal of quantised information) - removing information from a carrier is demodulation and decoding, which happen at the RECEIVER, not modulation.
D (filtering) - filtering removes unwanted frequency components to clean up a signal; it is a refinement step, not the addition of information to a carrier.
1 mark: identifies modulation as the addition of information to a carrier wave

content.text: Which row of the table correctly describes the property changes that occur after tempering quench-hardened steel?
Toughness: Increased; Hardness: Minimal loss
Toughness: Minimal loss; Hardness: Increased
Toughness: Increased; Hardness: Increased
Toughness: Minimal loss; Hardness: Minimal loss

Quench-hardened steel is extremely hard and extremely brittle. Tempering is a low-temperature reheat used to relieve the internal stresses responsible for that brittleness, so think about which property has to be recovered and which one is deliberately traded away.
The tempering temperature is chosen well below the eutectoid, so the property changes are a moderate adjustment of the quenched structure, not a wholesale loss of hardness.
A
Row A is correct: toughness increased, hardness minimal loss.

Quenching from above the eutectoid temperature traps carbon in a supersaturated, distorted body-centred tetragonal martensite lattice. This gives very high hardness but leaves large internal stresses and a very low impact toughness, so the quenched component is brittle and prone to cracking.

Tempering reheats the component to a temperature well below the eutectoid (commonly $200$ to $650^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$), which precipitates carbides from the martensite, relieves the internal stresses and allows some retained austenite to transform. The material therefore regains ductility and impact toughness. Because the temperature is kept low, only a modest fraction of the hardness is given up - hardening tools are routinely tempered and remain hard.

items: B (minimal loss of toughness, hardness increased) - this reverses the effect. Tempering always reduces hardness and increases toughness relative to the as-quenched condition.
C (increased toughness, increased hardness) - impossible. Carbon precipitation and stress relief always soften the martensite, so hardness cannot rise during tempering.
D (minimal loss of both) - wrong because a substantial increase in toughness is the entire purpose of tempering. It is only the loss of hardness that is kept small.
1 mark: recognises that tempering increases toughness and reduces hardness only slightly; selects the row showing increased toughness with minimal loss of hardness

questions.notes: Data defect (does not affect the key): the stored alt text is materially misleading for two options. It describes options B and D almost identically as two switches in series, which is not the discriminating feature. The source option images were inspected: B is two series switches in the top supply conductor (an AND circuit), whereas D is two series switches in a vertical branch that short-circuits the lamp when both are closed (a NAND circuit). The stored key D is correct.

content.text: Which of the following electronic circuits functions as a NAND logic gate?

content.alt_text: Circuit A: a battery with two switches connected in parallel in the top branch, driving a lamp.
Circuit B: a battery with two switches connected in series along the top conductor, driving a lamp.
Circuit C: a battery with a parallel pair of switches in one branch and a parallel pair in a second branch, driving a lamp.
Circuit D: a battery with two switches connected in series in a single branch, driving a lamp.

content.text: Write out the NAND truth table: the output is ON for every combination of inputs EXCEPT the one in which all inputs are ON.

With two switches as the inputs and the lamp as the output, decide what must happen when only ONE switch is closed, and then when BOTH are closed. The lamp must light in the first case and go out in the second. Consider not just switches in the supply conductor but a branch that can short-circuit part of the circuit when it is closed.
D
A NAND gate gives an output ON unless all inputs are ON. The correct circuit is option D.

In circuit D the two switches are in series with each other but that series combination forms a vertical branch connected ACROSS the top conductor. When both switches are open the branch carries nothing, the top conductor is continuous, and current flows through the lamp - output ON. When either switch alone is closed the output is still ON. Only when both are closed does the branch conduct and short-circuit the supply across the lamp, so no current flows through it and the lamp goes out - output OFF. That is exactly the NAND truth table.

items: A - the two switches are in parallel in the supply conductor, so the lamp lights whenever EITHER switch is closed. It is still lit when both are closed. That is OR, not NAND.
B - the two switches are in series along the top conductor, so the circuit is only completed when BOTH are closed; the lamp is out otherwise. That is AND, the opposite of NAND.
C - two parallel pairs in two branches short the supply whenever either pair is closed, so the lamp is lit only when all four switches are open. That is the NOR of the AND, not NAND.

1 mark: states the function of a NAND gate — output ON only when all inputs are OFF; identifies the series switch arrangement that completes the circuit unless both switches are closed; selects option D

assets.alt_text: Circuit A: a battery with two switches connected in parallel in the top branch, driving a lamp.
Circuit B: a battery with two switches connected in series along the top conductor, driving a lamp.
Circuit C: a battery with a parallel pair of switches in one branch and a parallel pair in a second branch, driving a lamp.
Circuit D: a battery with two switches connected in series in a single branch, driving a lamp.

content.text: Four output graphs from an oscilloscope are shown.

content.alt_text: Four voltage-time traces: Graph 1 is a symmetric alternating sine wave about $0\,\mathrm{V}$; Graph 2 is a rectified waveform between $0$ and $-V$; Graph 3 is a pulsating DC waveform between $0$ and $+V$; Graph 4 is a steady positive DC level.

content.text: Which of the graphs show direct current (DC)?
Graph 4 only
Graphs 3 and 4 only
Graphs 2, 3 and 4 only
Graphs 1, 2 and 3 only
The defining test is direction of flow: does the current REVERSE every half cycle, or does it always flow the same way through the load?

Read each trace against the time axis. A trace that swings both positive and negative is alternating; a trace that never crosses to the other side of the axis stays one-directional however much it ripples.
C
Direct current is any current that flows in one direction only through the load. Applying that test to each trace:

items: Graph 1 - the trace swings symmetrically between $+V$ and $-V$, reversing every half cycle. This is alternating current (AC), so it is excluded.
Graph 2 - the negative half of the sine has been retained and the positive half removed, so the trace lies entirely between $0$ and $-V$ and never changes sign. This is half-wave rectified DC.

Graph 3 - each negative half cycle has been flipped upwards, giving a train of positive humps between $0$ and $+V$ that never crosses the axis. This is full-wave rectified DC - it still flows one way only, so it is DC even though it is not steady.
Graph 4 - a constant positive potential. This is steady DC.

content.text: Direct current is therefore Graphs 2, 3 and 4 - option C.

items: A (Graph 4 only) - too narrow: it excludes the two rectified waveforms, which are also one-directional.
B (Graphs 3 and 4 only) - excludes Graph 2, which is just as one-directional as Graph 3, only negative.
D (Graphs 1, 2 and 3 only) - wrongly includes Graph 1, the one trace that reverses direction, and omits the steady DC in Graph 4.

1 mark: identifies Graph 1 as AC because the trace reverses about $0\,\mathrm{V}$; identifies Graphs 2 and 3 as unidirectional (rectified) DC; identifies Graph 4 as steady DC and selects Graphs 2, 3 and 4

content.text: Aircraft skins can be constructed using either fibre metal laminate (FML) or sheet aircraft-grade aluminium alloy. FML is preferred in this application because it has
higher density and lower Young's modulus.
higher density and improved fatigue resistance.
higher strength-to-weight ratio and lower Young's modulus.
higher strength-to-weight ratio and improved fatigue resistance.

Aircraft skins are weight-critical, so the comparison must be made on strength PER UNIT MASS rather than on strength alone. Any option claiming a higher density can be rejected immediately, because that is the opposite of a reason for choosing the material.

Then consider what fails first in a repeatedly loaded skin. A monolithic sheet has nothing to stop a crack growing right across it, whereas fibres bridge cracks and carry load around them. Also check whether stiffness per unit mass or absolute Young's modulus is the property that actually matters to the designer.
D
Option D - higher strength-to-weight ratio and improved fatigue resistance.

Fibre metal laminate (for example GLARE) consists of alternating layers of glass or carbon fibre prepreg and thin aluminium alloy sheets, bonded and cured. Most of the strength and stiffness comes from fibres whose density is roughly a third that of aluminium, so for a given load the laminate is considerably lighter than a monolithic sheet of the same thickness - a higher SPECIFIC strength, which is what matters on an aircraft.

The fibre plies also arrest cracks: a crack growing through an aluminium layer is bridged by the fibres, which carry load across the crack and force it to take a longer, more tortuous path. Delamination and residual stresses further spread the damage, so the fatigue life is much better than that of a plain sheet of the same thickness. Aircraft skins are in a constant cycle of pressurisation, taxiing and landing loads, so fatigue resistance is a decisive advantage.

items: A (higher density and lower Young's modulus) and B (higher density and improved fatigue resistance) - both claim a HIGHER density for FML, which is the reverse of the reason for choosing it.

C (higher strength-to-weight ratio and lower Young's modulus) - the specific strength is right but a lower Young's modulus is not an advantage. What the designer wants is high STIFFNESS PER UNIT MASS (a high specific modulus), not a lower absolute modulus.

1 mark: recognises that FML has a higher strength-to-weight ratio than sheet aircraft-grade aluminium alloy; recognises that the fibre layers improve fatigue resistance; selects the option combining both correct properties

content.text: The force $F$ is moved from joint $W$ to joint $X$, as shown.

content.alt_text: Two states of the same wall bracket: joints Y (pinned to a wall) and W (roller against the wall) with member $WX$; in the left frame $F$ acts down at $W$, in the right frame $F$ acts down at $X$.

content.text: Which option correctly shows what happens to the internal force in member $XY$ and the reaction force at $W$ when the force $F$ is moved from joint $W$ to joint $X$?
Internal force in member XY: Decreases; Reaction force at W: Decreases
Internal force in member XY: Increases; Reaction force at W: Increases
Internal force in member XY: Increases; Reaction force at W: Decreases
Internal force in member XY: Decreases; Reaction force at W: Increases

Use the supports. The pin at the wall can supply both a horizontal and a vertical reaction, but the roller at the wall can only push horizontally. Work out what is left to carry the applied force in each of the two frames.
Then take moments about the wall pin in each frame and ask whether the applied force has a moment arm at all. If it has none, the frame cannot tend to rotate and the roller has nothing to resist.
B
The bracket has a vertical member from the pin $Y$ to the roller $W$, a horizontal member from $W$ to $X$, and a diagonal member from $Y$ to $X$.

Left frame, $F$ acting down at $W$: $W$ sits directly below the pin $Y$, so $F$ has no moment arm about $Y$ and the frame has no tendency to rotate. Joint $X$ carries no external load, and the two members meeting there are not collinear, so both must be zero-force members - giving zero force in member $XY$. Horizontal equilibrium of the whole frame then makes the roller reaction at $W$ zero as well.

Right frame, $F$ acting down at $X$: $F$ now has a horizontal moment arm about $Y$, so the frame would rotate away from the wall. The only force with a moment arm about $Y$ is the horizontal roller reaction at $W$, so it must increase to balance the moment, $R_W = F \cdot \dfrac{d}{WY}$. Joint $X$ must now pass the load along to the supports, and vertical equilibrium there gives a tension in the diagonal member $XY$ of $F\dfrac{s}{h}$, where $s$ is the length of the diagonal and $h$ the height of $Y$ above the bar - so the force in member $XY$ rises from zero to a non-zero value.
Both quantities therefore increase, which is row B.

items: Row A (decreases, decreases) - both are already zero in the left frame, so they cannot decrease.
Row C (increases, decreases) - the roller reaction must increase to provide the balancing moment, not decrease.
Row D (decreases, increases) - the diagonal carries no load at all when $F$ is at $W$, so moving the load to $X$ can only increase it.

1 mark: recognises that with $F$ at $W$ there is no moment arm about $Y$, so member $XY$ carries no force; recognises that with $F$ at $X$ member $XY$ must carry an increasing compressive force; recognises that the reaction at $W$ increases as the force in member $WY$ increases, and selects row B

content.text: Which heat-treated metal is used for contact springs in electrical switches?
OFHC copper
Phosphor bronze
Copper beryllium
Tough pitched copper
A contact spring in a switch has to do two jobs at once: carry the current, and hold a spring force while resisting wear at the contact face. Look for the alloy that can reach BOTH requirements.

Of the copper alloys listed, consider which can be hardened by precipitation hardening to spring-grade hardness while keeping its electrical conductivity high. Pure copper is the most conductive of all but is far too soft to hold a spring force.
C
Copper beryllium (option C).

A copper-beryllium alloy is precipitation hardened by solution treatment, quenching and ageing. The beryllium forms fine precipitates that obstruct dislocation movement, raising the hardness and elastic limit to spring-steel levels (typically about $35$ to $40\,\mathrm{RHC}$) while retaining high electrical conductivity, good thermal conductivity and good corrosion resistance. That combination of spring properties plus conductivity is why it is the standard material for electrical contact springs, clips and connector contacts.

items: A (OFHC copper) - the most conductive of all, but very soft. It deforms plastically on the first contact and cannot maintain a spring force or resist wear.

B (phosphor bronze) - a copper-tin alloy with adequate spring strength and good fatigue resistance, but its conductivity is much lower than copper's, so it is used where the mechanical property is the priority and the current is small.
D (tough pitched copper) - deliberately kept soft and ductile for drawing and formability; far too weak for a contact spring.

1 mark: recognises that contact spring material needs both high electrical conductivity and high hardness/strength; identifies copper beryllium, which can be precipitation hardened to spring-grade properties; rejects tough pitched copper, which is too soft for contact springs

content.text: A box with weight $W$ and subject to a friction force $F$ is being pulled up an inclined plane by a force $P$.

content.alt_text: Block on an inclined plane showing $P$ up the slope, friction $F$ down the slope, weight $W$ vertically down, normal force $N$ and resultant force $R$ directed into the plane.

content.text: Which two forces can be combined into a single resultant contact reaction?
$P$ and $W$
$P$ and $N$
$F$ and $W$
$F$ and $N$
Split the forces into those the applied pull $P$ has to work against and those that arise from the contact between the block and the plane.

The two forces you want are the ones that combine to give the resultant $R$ drawn acting into the plane. Ask which pair are perpendicular and parallel to the surface respectively, and which of the two opposes the motion of the block.
D
The two forces are $F$ and $N$ - option D.

$N$ is the normal reaction exerted by the plane on the block, acting perpendicular to the surface. $F$ is the friction force at the contact surface, acting along the plane and opposing the motion of the block up the slope. Together they are the contact forces, and their resultant is the single force $R$ shown acting into the plane, inclined backwards from the normal by the angle of friction.

Note that $P$ and $W$ are not contact forces. $P$ is the applied effort and $W$ is the weight; they determine how big $N$ and $F$ have to be ($N = W\cos\theta - P\sin\theta$) but they are not the pair that produces the resultant at the contact.

items: A ($P$ and $W$) - both are external forces on the block, and neither is a contact reaction, so they cannot give the contact resultant $R$.
B ($P$ and $N$) - mixes the applied effort with the normal reaction; the friction force is omitted.
C ($F$ and $W$) - mixes a contact force with the weight; the normal reaction is omitted.

1 mark: identifies $N$ as the contact reaction perpendicular to the plane and $F$ as the friction force along the plane; recognises that their resultant $R$ acts into the plane opposing motion, giving option D

For the kinetic energy calculation, both values must be in SI units: the mass is given in tonnes and the speed in kilometres per hour.
For the logic circuit, write down in words what each gate's output is before you combine the gates, then check the combination against the stated braking conditions.

3 marks: part (b) — Outline the benefits of using electric motors to power self-driving vehicles.
3 marks: part (c) — The self-driving vehicle has a mass of $1.5$ tonnes and is travelling at $60\,\mathrm{km/h}$.

content.text: Innovations in global positioning systems (GPS) and sensor technologies are used in the operation of this vehicle.
Describe how both of these innovations are used in the control of the vehicle.
For each innovation, name the input it uses and what the vehicle does with the information it produces.
GPS answers 'where am I and where am I going?', while the sensors answer 'what is in the way?' Treat them as a pair of inputs to one control system, not two unrelated inventions.
The question asks how they are used in control, so finish by saying what the control system actually operates on the vehicle.
GPS uses triangulation to determine the vehicle's position on the surface of the earth. Sensors detect objects in the vehicle's path or its immediate environment in order to avoid collision.
Answer each innovation in the same three-step pattern so the detail marks are obvious.

items: GPS: satellites emit timing signals and a receiver in the vehicle measures the travel time of several of them. Trigonometry on the satellite positions gives the vehicle's latitude, longitude and altitude, and repeated fixes give its heading and speed. The control system uses this to locate the vehicle, plan and follow a route, and know when to turn.

Sensors: lidar, cameras, radar and ultrasonic transducers continuously monitor the vehicle's immediate environment and detect objects, their distance and their relative motion. This data is fused and passed to the control system, which classifies the object and its trajectory.

Control: the control system compares the sensed path ahead with the planned path, decides on a steering, throttle or braking correction, and operates the steering, propulsion and braking actuators. Overriding the driver's inputs is what removes human error, and it is the detection of obstacles that prevents collision.
3 marks: describes in detail how both innovations are used to control the movement of the vehicle
2 marks: describes in detail how one innovation is used to control the movement of the vehicle, OR describes the two innovations with limited detail
1 mark: provides some relevant information

content.text: Outline the benefits of using electric motors to power self-driving vehicles.
Think about the whole energy chain: where the electricity comes from, and what the drivetrain has to do in an automated vehicle.
A benefit of electric motors here is partly a systems or environmental benefit, not just a performance one, so include the effect on emissions.
Three marks means three distinct, developed points rather than one point explained at length.

Electric motors allow increased use of renewable energy, reducing atmospheric particulate matter. They also give an improved power-to-weight ratio, decreased noise pollution and are easier to integrate into an automated vehicle control system.
Develop three separate benefits and make each one explicit about why electric motors deliver it.

items: Renewable energy: a battery electric vehicle can be charged from renewable generation, so it allows increased use of renewable energy and reduces atmospheric particulate matter compared with an internal combustion engine.

Power-to-weight ratio: electric motors deliver their rated power immediately and can be placed close to the driven wheels, giving a better power-to-weight ratio and removing the need for a multi-speed gearbox, which reduces vehicle mass.
Noise: electric motors are almost silent, so the vehicle produces much less noise pollution, which matters most in urban and residential areas.
Integration: motors and their power electronics are easy to command precisely, so they integrate directly with the automated control system that steers, drives and brakes a self-driving vehicle.
3 marks: outlines the benefits of using electric motors to power self-driving vehicles
2 marks: identifies the benefits of using electric motors to power self-driving vehicles
1 mark: provides some relevant information

content.text: The self-driving vehicle has a mass of $1.5$ tonnes and is travelling at $60\,\mathrm{km/h}$. Calculate its kinetic energy.
Kinetic energy is $KE = \tfrac{1}{2}mv^{2}$, and both values must be in SI units. The mass is given in tonnes and the speed in kilometres per hour.
Convert $60\,\mathrm{km/h}$ to $\mathrm{m/s}$ by dividing by $3.6$, not by $3.6 \times 1000$.
A $1500\,\mathrm{kg}$ mass travelling at $16.7\,\mathrm{m/s}$ stores energy of order $2 \times 10^{5}\,\mathrm{J}$, so the final answer will be of order a couple of hundred kilojoules.
$208.4\,\mathrm{kJ}$
$v = 60\,\mathrm{km/h} = \dfrac{60\times1000}{3600} = 16.67\,\mathrm{m/s}$
$m = 1.5\,\mathrm{t} = 1500\,\mathrm{kg}$

items: 3 marks: calculates the correct value of kinetic energy with relevant working
2 marks: calculates the kinetic energy using a correct method but with minor errors
1 mark: applies an appropriate formula OR converts relevant values

content.text: Digital logic controls the vehicle's brakes.

content.alt_text: Detail of the vehicle front showing sensors 1 and 2, one at the front bumper and one on the rear flank.

content.text: Brakes will be applied when all of the following conditions are met:

items: the motor is on
the vehicle is in motion
either sensor 1 or sensor 2 is activated.

content.text: Explain how the logic gates, labelled 1, 2 and 3 in the circuit below, control the vehicle's brakes.

content.alt_text: Logic circuit: 'Motor engine on' and 'Vehicle in motion' feed gate 1 (AND); 'Sensor 1 activated' and 'Sensor 2 activated' feed gate 2 (OR); the outputs of gates 1 and 2 feed gate 3 (AND) which drives 'Brakes applied'.

content.text: Read the shape of each gate off the circuit first, then say in words what its output is when its inputs change.
Notice that only one of the three stated conditions is an 'either/or'. That gate must be an OR, not an AND.
The brakes respond to the combination of the two gate outputs, so the final gate decides whether the two groups of conditions must be met together.

Gate 1 is an AND gate that produces an ON output only when both the motor is on and the vehicle is in motion. Gate 2 is an OR gate that produces an ON output when either sensor 1 or sensor 2 is activated. Gate 3 is an AND gate, so the brakes are applied only when gate 1 and gate 2 outputs are both ON.
Work through the circuit from the inputs towards the brakes, one gate at a time.

items: Gate 1 takes 'motor engine on' and 'vehicle in motion' and is an AND gate, so its output is ON only when both inputs are ON; if either the motor is off or the vehicle is stationary, gate 1 blocks the output.

Gate 2 takes 'sensor 1 activated' and 'sensor 2 activated' and is an OR gate, so its output is ON if either sensor alone is activated, which covers an obstacle detected at the front bumper or at the rear flank.
Gate 3 takes the outputs of gates 1 and 2 and is an AND gate, so 'brakes applied' goes ON only when both gate outputs are ON.

Overall: the brakes are applied only when the motor is on, the vehicle is moving, and at least one sensor has detected a hazard. Any single missing condition holds the brakes off, which is the fail-safe behaviour required.
3 marks: explains how the three logic gates act together to control the brakes of the vehicle
2 marks: explains how the logic gates act together to control the brakes of the vehicle but with minor errors
1 mark: provides some relevant information

content.text: Work across the table one row at a time and first decide which of the three columns the blank sits in: a material, a property or a process. The two entries already given in each row are the clues for the missing one.

content.text: Each blank is filled by asking what the other two columns in that row already demand.

items: Tyre, material: the property column requires flexibility and a high coefficient of friction, and rubber is the only common material with both, so rubber. Compression moulding then forces the rubber into the tread pattern.

Axle, property: the axle is a machined alloy steel component that carries the whole vehicle load in bending and takes the shock of every pothole, so hardness (to resist wear) and toughness (to resist fracture) are the required properties.
Light cover, method: acrylic is a thermoplastic, and the standard forming process for a complex transparent cover is injection moulding, which also gives a smooth surface and accurate repeatability.
Chassis, property: a rolled mild steel chassis member must resist bending without deflecting under the vehicle loads, so stiffness/rigidity is the required property.

Body panels, material: hand lay-up of a resin is the manual process used for fibre reinforced plastics, so the material is GRP, glass reinforced polymer. The resilience (springiness) then allows the panel to survive impacts.
Electrical wire, method: copper cannot be cast or moulded into a continuous fine wire; it is drawn, pulled through a die to reduce the cross-section and to work-harden and refine the copper.

content.text: The chassis for the vehicle could be made from a solid steel bar or hollow steel tube. Both the bar and the tube have the same mass and cost per metre.

content.alt_text: A solid steel bar and a hollow steel tube of the same mass, labelled as candidates for the vehicle chassis.

content.text: Justify why a hollow tube would be used in preference to a solid bar to build the vehicle chassis.
The mass and the cost per metre are given as identical, so neither can decide the choice. The comparison has to be made on a property of the shape rather than of the material.

Compare the two sections on how far the material sits from the axis about which the chassis bends: bending resistance for a given mass depends on the distribution of that mass, not on the total amount of it.
There is also a non-structural reason for choosing the hollow section - think about what can be run along the inside of it and how that changes the design of the vehicle.

The hollow steel tube is more rigid because it has a greater second moment of area than the solid steel bar. This rigidity is important in the chassis as it is subjected to continual flexural forces and moments when in use, so stiffness is an important design requirement. Additionally, cables for the electrics can be fed along the axis of the hollow tube and be protected from damage.
Step 1 - identify the design requirement. A vehicle chassis is loaded in bending every time it travels, so the requirement is stiffness, not strength: deflection, not fracture, limits the design.

Step 2 - identify the governing section property. Stiffness in bending is governed by the second moment of area, $I = \int y^{2}\,\mathrm{d}A$, so every part of the cross-section counts according to the square of its distance from the neutral axis. A section that uses the same amount of steel but places it further from the axis therefore has a much larger $I$.

Step 3 - apply to the two candidates. A solid bar of a given mass has all of its material close to the neutral axis, so its $I$ is small. A hollow tube of the same mass has two thin walls standing well away from the axis, so its $I$ is many times larger and its deflection under the same load is correspondingly smaller. This is the justification the marking guideline requires.

Step 4 - add the design benefit. The hollow core can also carry the electrical wiring along the axis of the tube, where it is shielded from impact and from the weather, removing the need for a separate cable route.

items: 3 marks: justifies the use of the hollow tube, including reference to second moment of area and other relevant engineering or design features
2 marks: provides an engineering or design reason that supports the use of the hollow tube
1 mark: provides some relevant information

content.text: What force $Q$ is required to overcome the $20\,\mathrm{N}$ resistance force shown?
Treat the bearing as the pivot. The $20\,\mathrm{N}$ resistance acts through the bearing, so it has no moment about the bearing axis, and only $Q$ produces a turning moment.

The view is drawn to scale, so measure the perpendicular distance from the centre of the bearing to the line of action of $Q$ on the figure, and measure the moment arm of the $20\,\mathrm{N}$ force the same way. Keep both in the same units before substituting.
Sanity check: $Q$ is applied further out from the axis than the resisting force, so it should come out smaller than $20\,\mathrm{N}$.
Taking moments about the centre of the bearing, the moment arm $d$ is scaled from the drawing.

items: 3 marks: calculates the force Q accurately using a correct method, including the correct moment arm scaled from the drawing
2 marks: calculates the force Q using a correct method but with minor errors
1 mark: applies an appropriate method

content.text: The components of the bearing assembly used in the fidget spinner are shown.
The retainer can be made from either glass fibre-reinforced nylon or stainless steel.
Compare the in-service properties of these materials for use in the retainer.

A comparison needs at least one property for each material, and for each property the effect it has while the retainer is in service. A list of properties with no consequence attached scores the lower band only.
Think about the environment the retainer works in: grease and solvents, high rotational speed, heat, and shock or vibration loading.
Watch the extremes of temperature and moisture: one of these materials changes character well before the other does, and that is the argument that decides the choice.

Both GFRN and stainless steel have excellent corrosion resistance and are resistant to a wide range of organic solvents and greases used in bearings. Nylon on steel has a much lower coefficient of friction than steel-on-steel, so GFRN bearings produce far less heat from friction, run at higher speeds and produce lower noise levels. Stainless steel has a far wider range of operating temperatures than GFRN (which softens at high temperature and turns brittle at low temperature), so it better resists shock loading or vibration.
Method: treat the two materials in the same order — property, then service consequence — so the points pair up as a comparison, then finish with a decision.

items: Stainless steel: high corrosion resistance and good resistance to the organic solvents and greases used with bearings, so it will not seize or contaminate the lubricant; a very wide operating temperature range; tough, so it tolerates shock and vibration loading.

Glass fibre reinforced nylon: also corrosion resistant and unaffected by those greases and solvents, so both materials survive the same chemical environment — this is the similarity in the comparison.

Glass fibre reinforced nylon against steel has a much lower coefficient of friction than steel against steel, so less energy is converted to heat, less lubricant is needed, the bearing can run at higher speeds and the running noise is much lower.

Glass fibre reinforced nylon is temperature limited: it softens when hot and becomes brittle when cold, whereas stainless steel retains its properties over a far wider range, so stainless steel is the better choice where shock, vibration or extreme temperature is expected.
A response that lists properties only, or that discusses only one of the two materials, cannot score the comparison marks.
4 marks: provides a detailed comparison of the suitability of both materials for use as a bearing retainer
3 marks: describes the suitability of each material for use as a bearing retainer
2 marks: outlines at least one of the materials
1 mark: provides some relevant information
